entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Heracles in Rome (Aedes Herculis Victoris, 'Temple of Hercules Victor'), located in the Forum Boarium (Rome's ancient cattle market near the Tiber River), is one of the best-preserved examples of ancient Roman circular temple architecture in the world — dating to the late 2nd or early 1st century BCE (circa 120-100 BCE), built in the Corinthian order with 20 (originally) columns surrounding a circular cella, and surviving largely intact because it was continuously used as a church (Santo Stefano and later Santa Maria del Sole) from the early medieval period.

Heracles (Hercules) had particular associations with Rome's Forum Boarium: ancient traditions credited Hercules with passing through this area during his cattle-driving labors (the Tenth Labor, recovering Geryon's cattle), and the merchant community (particularly olive oil merchants) regarded him as their patron. The circular Corinthian temple — built from fine Pentelic marble imported from Greece — represents the highest artistic quality of late Republican Roman religious architecture, comparable to the Pantheon's later structural ambition.

The temple's survival is attributable to Christianization: it was converted to Christian use and the name 'Santa Maria del Sole' (Holy Mary of the Sun) was given when a golden statue of a figure (probably Hercules or possibly a sun deity) was discovered in the Tiber nearby. The temple's near-complete preservation of its colonnade makes it invaluable for understanding late Republican Corinthian temple design and Roman circular temple typology. Today it stands in the middle of the Forum Boarium piazza alongside the square Temple of Portunus, constituting Rome's best-preserved cluster of Republican-era temples.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Heracles in Rome — best-preserved circular Roman Republican temple in existence, surviving through medieval Christianization as 'Santa Maria del Sole,' and constituting with the Temple of Portunus Rome's most intact Republican religious precinct — is an invaluable primary source for ancient Roman sacred architecture.
